title: Scaled dot-product attention
subtitle: Edit small Q, K and V matrices and follow softmax(QK<sup>T</sup> / √d<sub>k</sub>) V step by step.

intro.idea: Attention lets each query look at a set of keys, decide how relevant each key is, and return a weighted average of the matching values. Relevance is the dot product of query and key. A softmax turns each query's scores into weights that are positive and sum to 1.
intro.why: It is the core operation of the Transformer: every token builds its output by mixing information from other tokens, with mixing weights computed from the data itself. The √d<sub>k</sub> scaling keeps the scores in a range where the softmax still responds smoothly as d<sub>k</sub> grows.
steps: Scores: S = Q K<sup>T</sup>. Entry (i, j) is the dot product of query i with key j.
Scale: divide every score by √d<sub>k</sub> (switch this off to compare).
Weights: apply a softmax to each row, A<sub>ij</sub> = exp(S<sub>ij</sub>) / Σ<sub>j'</sub> exp(S<sub>ij'</sub>). Each row sums to 1.
Output: O = A V. Row i of O is the weighted average of the value rows, using row i of A as weights.

symbols.meaning: values, one row per key (paired with K)

visuals.title: Step 1–2 · Scores fed to the softmax (QK<sup>T</sup>, scaled if on)
visuals.caption: Row = query, column = key. Larger means the query and key point in more similar directions.

visuals.title: Step 3 · Attention weights A = softmax per row
visuals.caption: Each row is a probability distribution over keys. The right column confirms each row sums to 1.

visuals.title: Query q1: scores vs. weights
visuals.caption: The softmax keeps the order of the scores but squashes them into weights that sum to 1. Bigger gaps between scores give a more one-sided distribution.

visuals.title: Step 4 · Output O = A V
visuals.caption: Each output row is a blend of the value rows. Compare it with V on the left.

explorations.title: Equal scores give a plain average
explorations.change: Press Try it: the query is all zeros. Then change K freely.
explorations.observe: Every score is 0, every weight is 1/3 ≈ 0.333, and the output is the plain mean of the value rows, (2, 2). Changing K does not change anything while q1 = 0.
explorations.why: A zero query has dot product 0 with every key. The softmax of equal numbers is uniform, so the output is an unweighted average of V.

explorations.title: A dominant score, and what the √d<sub>k</sub> scaling does (and does not) do
explorations.change: Press Try it: q1 matches k1 strongly. Read the weight of k1, then switch off the √dk scaling.
explorations.observe: With scaling the weight on k1 is about 0.894. Without it, it rises to about 0.965, and the output moves closer to v1 = (1, 0). The winning key stays the same.
explorations.why: Dividing by √d<sub>k</sub> shrinks the gaps between scores, so the softmax is less extreme. A common misconception is that scaling changes which key wins: it never changes the order, only how sharp the weights are. The paper motivates the factor for large d<sub>k</sub> with random, unit-variance components; for hand-picked toy vectors like these it is simply a fixed divisor.

limitations: Q, K and V are typed in directly. In a Transformer they are learned linear projections of token embeddings; no training happens here.
This is single-head attention without masking. Multi-head attention runs several of these in parallel and concatenates the outputs.
The scaling argument in the paper assumes query and key components are independent with mean 0 and variance 1. Small hand-picked matrices do not satisfy this.
The softmax uses the max-subtraction trick for numerical stability. This changes no result; it only avoids overflow for large scores.

source.equation: Attention(Q, K, V) = softmax( Q K<sup>T</sup> / √d<sub>k</sub> ) V

supported.claim: Each query is compared with every key using a dot product, and a softmax produces the weights on the values.
supported.quote: apply a softmax function to obtain the weights on the values

supported.claim: The dot products are divided by √d<sub>k</sub>.
supported.quote: We compute the dot products of the query with all keys, divide each by

supported.claim: For large d<sub>k</sub>, unscaled dot products grow large and push the softmax into regions with very small gradients.
supported.quote: pushing the softmax function into regions where it has extremely small gradients

simplifications: We use tiny matrices (at most 4 queries, 5 keys, d<sub>k</sub> ≤ 4) with values you type in, instead of learned projections.
The scaling on/off switch is a teaching device for comparison; the paper always scales.
The example matrices, presets and the max-subtraction softmax are our own choices.
